about.title: Banning Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Banning's mix of shopping centers along Ramsey Street, apartment complexes, and small businesses near the I-10 corridor means plenty of foot traffic across parking lots, stairwells, and store aisles every day. When a property owner lets a hazard sit unaddressed — a spill left too long, a cracked walkway, a broken handrail — the person who falls often pays the price in medical bills and missed work. California law asks whether the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the danger and failed to fix or warn about it. That's why what happens right after a fall matters: photos of the hazard, names of witnesses, and a request to preserve any surveillance footage can make a real difference later. LawProactive doesn't practice law ourselves, but we can connect you with an independent attorney familiar with Riverside County premises cases who will review what happened and explain your options at no upfront cost.

items.title: Notice Is the Key Question
items.desc: California premises cases hinge on whether the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney can help identify inspection records, maintenance logs, or prior complaints that speak to that notice.

items.title: Video and Evidence Disappear Fast
items.desc: Store and apartment surveillance systems often overwrite footage within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request preservation of that video can be critical to showing what really happened.

items.title: Comparative Fault Doesn't Bar You
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, you can still pursue a claim even if you're found partly responsible for the fall — your recovery is simply adjusted accordingly, not eliminated.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Banning?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a premises liability lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a government entity, such as a city facility, the deadline is much shorter and requires an early claim to be filed. An attorney can confirm the exact timeline for your situation.

items.question: What if I fell on a business's property along Ramsey Street or near I-10?
items.answer: Commercial properties in high-traffic areas like Banning's Ramsey Street corridor still owe visitors a duty to maintain safe conditions and address known hazards. The same legal standards for notice and reasonable care apply whether the fall happened at a large retailer or a small local shop. An independent attorney can help sort out who was responsible for maintaining the specific area where you fell.

items.question: Will I have to prove the property owner knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Yes, showing notice is usually central to a California premises liability claim — either the owner actually knew about the dangerous condition or should have discovered it through reasonable inspection. This is why documenting the hazard, taking photos, and identifying witnesses right away can matter so much. An attorney can help gather evidence that supports this element of your claim.
